title: Team Members Who See Their Role as Just a Job
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article contrasts team members who see their current position as merely a job with those who see it as a stepping stone in a career, arguing the latter group invests more emotionally, develops skills faster, and takes more pride in their work. The author outlines how leaders can shift this framing: walking people through potential career paths, mapping the specific skills and experiences needed for advancement, and connecting daily work to the organization's larger mission. The piece notes this reframing matters even where advancement opportunities are limited, since the goal is preparing people for wherever the future takes them, not guaranteeing promotion.
points: Team members who frame their current position as a step in a career, rather than just a job, invest more emotional energy, develop skills more aggressively, and take more pride in their work.
Leaders can shift this framing by walking people through potential career paths and mapping the specific skills, experiences, and relationships needed for advancement.
Even in organizations with limited advancement opportunities, leaders can still cultivate a career mindset by preparing people for wherever the future takes them.
Connecting current work to organizational mission helps team members see their contribution as consequential rather than transactional.
quotes: Team members who view their work and role as a job operate very differently from those who see their current position as a stepping stone in a career.

Career-minded team members invest more emotional energy in their work, develop their skills more aggressively, engage with work and colleagues more actively, and take more pride in their accomplishments.
Good leaders promote a career orientation by engaging team members in planning for their future.

This is best done by working with them to map out the actionable steps to achieve advancement. The skills they must acquire or develop, the experiences they must realize, and the relationships they must nurture are all part of this mapping.
People who do “jobs” are generally more detached and transactional. They seldom own problems or go above and beyond to create quality outcomes.
